# Introduction and motivation

## Background and caveats

* I have been involved with technical assessments of DiRAC RAC applications for
  the last 4 years.
* All of what I'll say directly relates to the technical assessment for DiRAC
  RAC applications.
* Most of it should be applicable to applications to other providers such as
  * EuroHPC
  * UKRI National Compute Resources (NCR)
  * etc.

## Why do I need to provide this information?

* We want to be able to:
  * Understand whether your project/applications will be a good fit for the
    requested resources.
  * Work out whether alternative resources might be more appropriate.
  * Ensure that resources are used efficiently and effectively.
  * Fairly balance the resources when the total demand exceeds what's available.
  * Identify opportunities for potential RSE support in order to increase the
    efficiency of compute resources (more science per resource hour).

# Scaling and performance

## Strong scaling, weak scaling and profiling {.smaller}

* Amount of computational resource can be number of CPU cores/GPUs/nodes.
* Sometimes, only one of strong/weak scaling is relevant (e.g. if problem sizes
  are fixed).

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="33%"}
### Strong scaling

* Measures how time to solution/speed-up varies for a fixed problem size as the
  amount of computational resources increases.
* Usually compared to the smallest resource size.
* Ideal/perfect: Increasing resources by a factor of $n$ gives an $n\times$ 
  speed-up.
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
### Weak scaling

* Measures how time to solution varies as the problem size per unit of
  resource is held constant.
* Ideal/perfect: The time to solution is constant as the amount of resources is
  varied.
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
### Profiling

* Measures how software behaves at runtime. Can cover many aspects including:
  * CPU usage
  * Memory usage
  * Communication
  * GPU usage
  * Time spent in routines/functions
:::

::::

## Strong scaling {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
* Either:
  * Choose a representative problem size for your project.
  * If your problem size varies, construct a problem size that fills as much of
    the available resources (i.e. memory) for the smallest computational resource
    size you are testing (e.g. a full node).
* Plot on a log-log scale as this makes the ideal scaling a straight line.
* Here I have also plotted the _scaling efficiency_ which is the
  percentage of the ideal speedup achieved (ideally only want to run in >50-70%
  efficiency regime).
* Drop/tailing off in scaling performance is inevitable as resources increase.
* Small bumps or jumps are also fine.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![Strong scaling results for GRTeclyn on Tursa. The blue line with circle
  markers is the measured walltimes of the evolution (left vertical axis scale).
  The dashed orange line is the ideal (or perfect) strong scaling walltimes
  starting from the measured walltime on 1 node. The green line with square
  markers is the scaling efficiency (right vertical axis
  scale)](media/grteclyn-strong-scaling-tursa.svg)
:::

::::

## Weak scaling {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
* This is relevant if problem sizes (e.g. resolution) are not fixed.
* For the smallest resource size, start with a problem size that fills as much
  of the available resources (i.e. memory) as possible.
* As the number of resources increases, increase the problem size proportionally
  so that the work per unit of resource remains the same.
  * For example, when you double the number of cores, you could double the
    length of the grid(s) in a single dimension.
* Again, small bumps are fine and some drop in scaling is normal.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![Weak scaling plot taken from the [DiRAC Scalability Training
Course](https://training-academy.dirac.ac.uk/course/view.php?id=29)](media/dirac-training-weak-scaling.png)
:::

::::

## Considerations for scaling

* Run on the same system/architecture you are applying for (or as close as
  possible). DiRAC guidance says within the last 5 years.
* Ideally have at least 4 different resource sizes.
* Generally easiest to double the number of resources from the base (e.g. 64,
  128, 256, 512 cores).
* Be explicit in describing your problem sizes used for scaling plots and how
  they relate to the problem sizes you intend to run as part of your project.
* Label and caption your plots clearly!
* Best to show both a plot and a table of results.
